beginner: Plant cantaloupe in light, well-drained soil that warms up fast, like a sandy loam, with some compost mixed in. Go easy on rich, high-nitrogen material, because that gives you lots of leaves and vine but less fruit and lower sugar. Many gardeners plant on low hills or raised mounds, which warm up and drain better and keep the fruit off soggy ground. If your soil is heavy clay, it stays cold and wet and can bring on disease, so mix in compost and build the soil up into mounds, or pick the sandiest, best-draining spot you have.
seasoned: Cantaloupe does best in deep, well-drained, light soil, with sandy loams and loamy sands the classic choice because they warm quickly in spring and drain freely, which this heat-loving, warm-season vine rewards with earlier, sweeter fruit. Work a few inches of compost or well-rotted manure into the bed before planting, but go easier on high-nitrogen amendments than you would for leafy crops, since too much nitrogen pushes vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Many growers plant on low, wide hills or raised mounds, which warm faster, drain better, and lift the crown and developing fruit off wet ground. Heavy clay holds water and stays cold, slowing growth and inviting Fusarium wilt and fruit rot, so amend it generously and build mounds, or grow on sandier ground.

beginner: Cantaloupe likes soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.
seasoned: Cantaloupe grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.8, with extension melon guides most often citing a 6.0 to 6.5 sweet spot. It tolerates a somewhat wider band, but strongly acidic or strongly alkaline soil tightens nutrient uptake and can worsen blossom-end and nutrient problems. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.

beginner: Cantaloupe does not need a lot of nitrogen, and too much gives you big leafy vines but fewer, less sweet melons. Mix a fertilizer that is lower in nitrogen, like a 5-10-10, into the soil before planting, then give the plants a little nitrogen before the vines start to run and again after the flowers bloom. Once the melons start to form, stop pushing nitrogen so the plant puts its energy into growing sweet fruit instead of more leaves.
seasoned: Cantaloupe is a moderate feeder that wants more phosphorus and potassium than nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Work a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson suggests about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then side-dress with a nitrogen source before the vines start to run, and again lightly after bloom as fruit develops. Ease off nitrogen once fruit has set so the plant pours its energy into sizing and sweetening the melons rather than growing more vine. Pair feeding with even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.

beginner: Your cantaloupe vines are starting to spread. Give them a light feeding of nitrogen now.
seasoned: Your cantaloupe vines are about to run, time to side-dress with a little nitrogen. Then feed again lightly after bloom, and ease off nitrogen once fruit sets so the plant builds sweet melons rather than vine.

beginner: Use a lower-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 at planting, then a little nitrogen as the vines start to spread. Do not overdo the nitrogen once melons form, or you get leaves instead of fruit.
seasoned: A lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress before the vines run and again lightly after bloom, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets. Too much nitrogen gives vine and leaf at the expense of fruit and sweetness.

beginner: Mix a lower-nitrogen fertilizer or a few inches of compost into the soil before planting. Then feed with a little nitrogen before the vines run, scratched into the soil a few inches away from the plants, and once more after the flowers bloom.
seasoned: A common approach is a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked into the bed before planting (Clemson cites about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then a nitrogen side-dress before the vines run, such as calcium nitrate at about 2 pounds of 15.5-0-0 per 100 feet of row placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeated lightly after bloom as fruit develops.

beginner: The most useful cantaloupe companions are flowers that bring in bees, since cantaloupe needs plenty of bee visits to set fruit. Nasturtiums can lure cucumber beetles away, which is worth doing because those beetles spread a wilt disease that hits cantaloupe hard. Bush beans add a little nitrogen. The one rule that really matters is to keep cantaloupe away from other melons, cucumbers, and squash, which all share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most cantaloupe companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on serve two practical ends: pollination and pest pressure. Because cantaloupe fruit set is strongly pollinator-limited, flowering insectary plants like borage near the patch are a genuine help. A trap planting of nasturtium can divert cucumber beetles, which matters more for cantaloupe than for most cucurbits, since muskmelon is highly susceptible to the bacterial wilt those beetles carry. Bush beans fix nitrogen the crop can use without the heavy feeding that would otherwise grow vine over fruit. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep cantaloupe away from other cucurbits, which share its pest and disease complex, including cucumber beetle and bacterial wilt, the mildews, and the soilborne Fusarium wilt and foliar gummy stem blight and Alternaria that build up where melons follow melons.

beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and cantaloupe needs plenty of bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination.
seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators cantaloupe fruit set depends on, since each female flower needs many bee visits to set a well-shaped, sweet melon. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-cantaloupe pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near melons and squash to lure cucumber beetles and other pests away, and their flowers bring in bees. For cantaloupe this matters extra, because cucumber beetles spread a wilt disease that hits it hard.
seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for cucumber beetles, and its flowers also draw the bees cantaloupe depends on for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, and it earns extra value here because cantaloupe is highly susceptible to the bacterial wilt cucumber beetles vector, though the specific nasturtium-cantaloupe effect is not formally isolated.

beginner: Beans pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which cantaloupe can use, and they do not share cantaloupe's pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
seasoned: Bush beans fix nitrogen that lightly benefits the crop without the heavy nitrogen that would push vine over fruit, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

beginner: Corn is the traditional Three Sisters partner that gives sprawling vines something to grow among. With cantaloupe it is more tradition than a proven boost, and cantaloupe's full-sun need means you should not let corn shade it much.
seasoned: The classic Three Sisters partner, though the fit is looser for cantaloupe than for shade-tolerant squash: tall corn can give the trailing vines structure, but cantaloupe wants full sun and heat to sweeten, so keep corn from shading the patch. A long-standing intercropping tradition with a space rationale, not a measured yield effect for this pair.

beginner: Keep cantaloupe away from other melons, cucumbers, and squash. They share most of the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
seasoned: Cucumber, watermelon, squash, and pumpkin share cantaloupe's pest and disease complex, including cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it carries, aphid-spread mosaic viruses, the mildews, and the soilborne Fusarium wilt and foliar gummy stem blight and Alternaria that build up where cucurbits repeat. Grouping them concentrates that pressure. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them on a long cycle.

beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and melons apart, since both are hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucurbits compete heavily and that potatoes can harbor disease and attract pests near melons. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

beginner: Small yellow beetles with stripes or spots chew on the leaves and flowers of young plants and can scar the fruit. The real danger is the wilt disease they spread, which hits cantaloupe hard, so even a few beetles are worth taking seriously.
seasoned: Small striped or spotted yellow beetles chew young leaves, stems, flowers, and the rind of developing fruit. The far bigger threat is indirect: cucumber beetles transmit bacterial wilt, and cantaloupe is one of the most susceptible cucurbits to it, much more than watermelon, which is nearly immune. An infected plant wilts runner by runner and dies even in moist soil.

beginner: Cucumber beetles spend the winter as adults and move onto young plants early, gathering on small seedlings. As they feed they spread bacterial wilt, and young plants up to about the five-leaf stage are most at risk, so early protection matters most.
seasoned: Striped and spotted cucumber beetles feed on cucurbits and overwinter as adults, colonizing plants early and massing on small seedlings. They carry the bacterial wilt organism Erwinia tracheiphila in their gut and spread it through feeding wounds and feces; seedlings at the cotyledon to five-leaf stage are the most vulnerable window.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover from the start (take it off when flowers open so bees can reach them), pick beetles off by hand, and clear away weeds. Since cantaloupe catches wilt easily, keep beetle numbers low on young plants. Kaolin clay and yellow sticky traps help too.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with floating row cover from planting, removed at flowering for pollination, hand-pick beetles, and clear weeds that shelter them. Because cantaloupe is wilt-prone, keep beetle numbers very low on young plants, treating when beetles reach about one per plant. Kaolin clay and yellow sticky traps help; keep plants vigorous so they grow past the vulnerable stage.

beginner: Cover seedlings until they flower, keep them growing strong, clear away weeds and old plants, and do not plant where melons or squash grew last year. Focus on keeping beetles off the youngest plants.
seasoned: Exclude beetles from seedlings with row cover, keep plants growing fast, clear weeds and debris, and rotate away from where cucurbits grew. Aim control at the early-season colonizers before the five-leaf stage, since that is when wilt infection does the most damage.

beginner: Tiny soft insects gather under the leaves and on new growth, making leaves curl and yellow, often with a sticky film. They can also spread viruses that damage the plant.
seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often melon aphids, cluster on leaf undersides and growing tips, curling and yellowing the leaves and coating them in sticky honeydew that grows sooty mold. Beyond direct feeding, melon aphids transmit mosaic viruses (cucumber mosaic, watermelon mosaic, zucchini yellow mosaic) that mottle and distort the foliage and can ruin a crop.

beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck the plant's juices and multiply quickly, especially on soft, over-fed growth. The sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold, and they can carry plant viruses.
seasoned: Melon and other aphids suck sap and multiply rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on stressed or over-fertilized plants, and typically colonize once the vines begin to run. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold, and several species spread cucurbit mosaic viruses.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control; reflective mulch deters them from young plants.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work. A reflective mulch around young plants helps keep aphids away.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective or aluminum-foil mulch deters aphids from young plants.

beginner: The leaves get a fine yellow or bronze speckling, and in bad cases you see tiny webs underneath. Spider mites love hot, dry weather and can build up fast on cantaloupe in summer.
seasoned: Pale yellow and reddish-brown stippling appears on the upper sides of leaves, ranging from small specks to large whitish, stippled areas, and fine webbing shows on leaf undersides in bad infestations. Two-spotted spider mites explode in hot, dry weather, exactly cantaloupe's season, and heavy feeding bronzes and dries the foliage, cutting fruit size and sugar.

beginner: Tiny mites that thrive in hot, dry summers and multiply fast, especially after broad insecticide sprays kill the helpful bugs that normally keep them down. They feed on the undersides of the leaves.
seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites are tiny sap-feeders that proliferate during hot, dry weather and whose populations explode rapidly when their natural enemies are killed off by broad-spectrum sprays. They feed mostly on leaf undersides.

beginner: Spray the plants, especially the undersides of the leaves, with a strong stream of water, and treat with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if needed. Avoid spraying broad insecticides, which kill the good bugs that eat mites.
seasoned: Spray plants with a strong jet of water to dislodge mites and raise humidity, and apply insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough leaf-underside coverage before populations peak, repeating as needed. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides, which kill the predatory mites and insects that control them.

beginner: Keep plants watered so they are not stressed in the heat, and avoid spraying strong insecticides that kill helpful bugs. Check under the leaves during hot, dry weather and treat early if you see speckling.
seasoned: Keep plants well watered and not heat-stressed, since drought-stressed plants are hit hardest, and avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that wipe out natural enemies. Scout leaf undersides through hot, dry spells and act early.

beginner: Leaves get yellow spots, then brown and wilt, and you find clusters of shield-shaped gray-brown bugs and their bronze eggs under the leaves. Cantaloupe is not their favorite, but they can still bother young plants.
seasoned: Leaves develop yellow specks that brown and wilt, and heavily fed runners can wilt and turn brittle. Flat bronze egg clusters appear on leaf undersides along the veins, and gray-brown adults and pale nymphs cluster near the crown and under debris. Cantaloupe is less affected than winter squash, but young plants can still be hurt.

beginner: Squash bugs pierce the leaves and stems and suck out the juices, which makes the vines wilt. They hide in plant debris over winter and prefer squash to cantaloupe, but can still attack young plants.
seasoned: The squash bug feeds with piercing-sucking mouthparts on cucurbit foliage and stems, injecting saliva that wilts and browns the tissue. Adults overwinter in garden debris and prefer squash and pumpkin to cantaloupe.

beginner: Pick the bugs off by hand and scrape off the egg clusters under the leaves. A board laid on the ground overnight draws them underneath, then lift it in the morning and destroy them. Treat the young bugs with insecticidal soap.
seasoned: Hand-pick adults, crush the bronze egg masses on leaf undersides, and trap bugs by laying a board near the plants overnight, then lifting it in the morning and destroying the cluster underneath. Target young nymphs with insecticidal soap, since adults are tough to kill.

beginner: Clean up old vines after harvest so the bugs have nowhere to overwinter, move your melons around the garden each year, and check under the leaves for eggs early in the season.
seasoned: Clean up vines and debris at season's end to cut overwintering sites, rotate cucurbits, and scout leaf undersides for the bronze egg clusters from early in the season, acting before nymphs mature.

beginner: On many squash, a healthy plant suddenly wilts in summer with sawdust-like specks at a hole near the base of the stem, and a fat white grub inside. Cantaloupe rarely gets this, since the borer mostly leaves melons alone, but it is still worth a look.
seasoned: On susceptible squash a vine wilts suddenly in midsummer with sawdust-like frass oozing from a hole low on the stem and a fat white caterpillar inside. Cantaloupe is a fortunate exception: the borer rarely attacks melons or cucumber, so this collapse is uncommon, though heavy local pressure can occasionally produce damage.

beginner: A moth lays eggs at the base of squash stems in early summer and the grubs tunnel inside, but the moth strongly prefers thin-stemmed squash like zucchini and mostly leaves cantaloupe alone.
seasoned: The larva of the squash vine borer moth bores into thin-stemmed Cucurbita pepo squash; it largely avoids melons and cucumber, so cantaloupe planted near a borer-ravaged zucchini usually sails through untouched. Where pressure is severe, an occasional larva may still enter.

beginner: Cantaloupe seldom needs treatment. If you do find a borer, slit the stem with a knife, dig out the grub, and cover the spot with damp soil so it can re-root.
seasoned: Rarely needed on cantaloupe. If a borer does enter, slit the stem lengthwise, remove the larva, and bury that node under moist soil to re-root; remove badly damaged vines.

beginner: Growing cantaloupe is half the battle, since the borer mostly skips melons. If borers are bad where you live, cover young plants with a light row cover until they flower, then take it off so bees can pollinate.
seasoned: Choosing cantaloupe is itself most of the prevention, since the borer mostly avoids melons. Where pressure is severe, row cover from planting until flowering excludes the egg-laying moths, and tilling in late winter and rotating disrupts overwintering pupae.

beginner: A runner, then the whole plant, wilts and dies over a few days even though the soil is wet. If you cut a wilted stem and press the ends together then pull them apart, a sticky string of ooze pulls out. Cantaloupe catches this disease easily, much more than watermelon.
seasoned: Individual runners wilt suddenly and the whole plant collapses over a few days, even in moist soil, often just as the vines are running or fruit is sizing. A useful field test: cut a wilted stem, press the cut ends together and slowly draw them apart, and a sticky, stringy ooze strings out between them. Cantaloupe is among the most susceptible cucurbits, far more than watermelon, which is nearly immune.

beginner: The wilt is caused by bacteria that live inside cucumber beetles over winter and get into the plant when the beetles feed. So the disease follows the beetles, and young plants catch it most easily. Keeping beetles off cantaloupe, especially when it is small, is the main defense.
seasoned: Bacterial wilt is caused by Erwinia tracheiphila, which clogs the water-conducting tissue. It has no soil or seed stage that matters here: it survives the winter inside cucumber beetles and is introduced when the beetles feed, so the disease tracks the beetle. Seedlings are infected most readily, and cantaloupe's high susceptibility makes early beetle control the whole game.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy wilting plants. You cannot spray the disease away, so the answer is to keep the cucumber beetles that spread it off your plants.
seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy wilting plants promptly so they do not seed more beetles with bacteria. Management is entirely preventive and aimed at the vector: exclude and control cucumber beetles, especially on young plants.

beginner: The key is to keep cucumber beetles off the plants, especially when young: cover seedlings with a light row cover until they flower, and control beetles early. Clean up weeds and old vines. There are not many resistant varieties, so beetle control is the main defense.
seasoned: Control the vector: protect seedlings with row cover until flowering, keep cucumber beetle numbers very low from emergence through the five-leaf stage, treating at about one beetle per plant, and clear weeds and debris. Few home varieties carry useful resistance, so exclusion and early beetle control are the reliable tools.

beginner: A white, powdery coating spreads over the leaves until they yellow, brown, and die. The plant fades early, and the melons may not size up or sweeten well.
seasoned: White, powdery patches appear on the upper and lower leaf surfaces and stems, spreading until leaves yellow, brown, and die back ahead of schedule. Early defoliation cuts the season short, reduces fruit size and sugar, and exposes melons to sunscald.

beginner: A fungus that spreads on warm, humid days, especially where plants are crowded and air does not move well. It does not need wet leaves to take hold.
seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi thrive in warm conditions with high humidity but do not need leaf wetness, spreading by wind-blown spores. Crowded plantings, poor airflow, and shade worsen it, and it is a common late-season cucurbit disease.

beginner: Treat early, at the first white spots, with a labeled fungicide like sulfur or horticultural oil, and remove badly affected leaves. Water the soil, not the leaves.
seasoned: Treat at the first spots with a labeled fungicide such as sulfur or a horticultural oil or biofungicide, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst leaves. Avoid overhead watering. Once it is widespread, control is mostly damage limitation.

beginner: Pick resistant varieties, give plants plenty of room and full sun, water at the base, and start checking in midsummer, treating the first white spots early.
seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, space plants for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering. Scout from midsummer and treat at the first sign.

beginner: Yellow, angular patches show on top of the leaves with fuzzy gray-purple growth underneath, mostly in damp, humid weather. The spots brown and spread, and badly hit leaves can die quickly.
seasoned: Irregular to angular yellow to brown areas appear on the upper leaf surface, bounded by the leaf veins, with a grayish or purplish fuzzy spore growth on the undersides in humid weather. Lesions expand and several infected leaves can die within days, rapidly defoliating the vines and starving the fruit of sugar.

beginner: A mold-like disease that blows in on the wind during mild, rainy weather and needs wet leaves to infect. It can move through a planting quickly.
seasoned: Downy mildew is caused by the air-borne, fungus-like water mold Pseudoperonospora cubensis, which needs leaf wetness and humidity to infect and arrives on wind currents during mild, rainy stretches, often spreading north through the season from overwintering sites in the far South.

beginner: Open up the planting so leaves dry faster, remove the worst leaves, and use a labeled fungicide when wet weather sets in. Do not water over the leaves.
seasoned: Improve airflow, let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a labeled fungicide covering leaf undersides when conditions favor the disease. Avoid overhead irrigation, which keeps leaves wet.

beginner: Give plants room so air moves between them, water at the base, choose resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live, and watch closely in humid weather.
seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the soil line rather than overhead, choose resistant varieties where available, and start protective sprays when the disease is reported moving into your area. Scout closely in humid weather.

beginner: The leaves turn yellow and wilt, often on just one runner at first, and the plant dies even though the soil is wet. Cutting the stem shows brown streaks inside. It lives in the soil, not in beetles.
seasoned: Foliage turns yellow and wilts, often starting on one side or one runner, and infected plants decline and die soon after symptoms appear even though the soil is moist. A cut stem reveals browned, discolored vascular tissue. It is a damaging soilborne disease of cantaloupe and, unlike bacterial wilt, is not carried by beetles.

beginner: A soil fungus that specifically attacks cantaloupe and muskmelon, blocking the plant's water pipes so it wilts. It builds up in the soil and survives for years, so it is hard to rotate away from once established.
seasoned: Fusarium wilt of cantaloupe is caused by the soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. melonis, which is specific to muskmelon and clogs the water-conducting tissue. It thrives in warm soils and persists in soil for years; several races exist, and resistance covers only some of them, which is why rotation alone often fails.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. You cannot spray it away, so prevention is everything.
seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy wilting plants. Management is preventive and cultural, since fungicides do not control a soilborne vascular wilt.

beginner: Choose resistant varieties, do not grow cantaloupe in the same ground year after year, and keep plants healthy and not overwatered. Since the fungus lives in the soil for years, resistant varieties matter most where it is a problem.
seasoned: Plant resistant varieties, follow a long rotation out of cantaloupe and related cucurbits, and keep plants vigorous but not over-watered. Because the fungus persists in soil and rotation is only partly effective, resistant cultivars are the most reliable defense where the disease is established.

beginner: You see round black spots on the leaves and dark sunken patches on the stems, sometimes with a brown gummy ooze. The leaf spots grow fast into big tan blotches, and in warm, wet weather the vines can collapse.
seasoned: Round, black, wrinkled spots form on young leaves and dark, sunken, sometimes girdling lesions develop on the stems, often with a brown gummy ooze on the surface. Brownish circular leaf spots expand rapidly into large tan lesions, and a black rot can appear on the fruit. In warm, wet weather the foliage and vines can collapse quickly. It is one of the most destructive cucurbit diseases in the humid South.

beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather, especially in the South, and survives on seed and old plant debris. Long rainy spells make it move fast.
seasoned: Gummy stem blight is caused by the seed-borne fungus Didymella bryoniae (Stagonosporopsis), a warm-weather cucurbit disease driven by prolonged rainy periods and leaf wetness. It survives on seed and infected debris and is especially destructive in the humid Southeast.

beginner: Use a labeled fungicide at the first sign and remove the worst vines. Give plants room so air moves between them, and water at the base to keep the leaves dry.
seasoned: Start a protective fungicide schedule at the first sign, covering leaf undersides, and remove and destroy badly affected vines. Improve airflow, avoid overhead irrigation, and keep the foliage as dry as possible.

beginner: Pick resistant varieties and clean seed, rotate where you grow melons, give plants room, water at the base, and keep an eye out in warm, humid weather.
seasoned: Plant resistant varieties and clean seed, rotate cucurbits out of the bed for several years, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and avoid working among wet vines. Scout closely in warm, humid weather.

beginner: Small brown spots start on the older leaves and grow into larger tan-brown blotches, sometimes with rings like a target. As they spread the leaves die, starting with the oldest, which can leave the melons sun-exposed and less sweet.
seasoned: Small brown spots appear first on the older crown leaves and enlarge into tan-to-brown lesions, often with concentric rings and a yellow halo, that merge and kill large areas of leaf. Severe defoliation exposes the fruit to sunscald and cuts sugar, and the disease works from the oldest leaves outward.

beginner: A fungus that likes warm, humid, rainy weather and survives on old plant debris and seed. It is worse on stressed or older leaves.
seasoned: Alternaria leaf blight is caused by the fungus Alternaria cucumerina, favored by warm, humid, rainy weather and long leaf wetness. It overwinters on infected debris and seed and hits stressed or aging foliage hardest.

beginner: Treat early, at the first spots, with a labeled fungicide and remove badly affected leaves. Water the soil, not the leaves, and stay out of the patch when the vines are wet.
seasoned: Treat at the first spots with a labeled fungicide such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst-affected leaves. Avoid overhead watering and working among wet vines. Keep plants vigorous, since healthy foliage resists it better.

beginner: Choose resistant varieties and clean seed, rotate where you grow melons, water at the base, give plants room, and remove sick leaves early. Keep the plants healthy so the leaves hold up.
seasoned: Plant resistant varieties and disease-free seed, rotate cucurbits out of the bed for several years, water at the base, space for airflow, and start a protective spray schedule before the disease appears in wet seasons. Keep plants well fed and watered so foliage stays vigorous.

beginner: Do not plant cantaloupe where you grew cucumbers, melons, squash, or pumpkins in the last few years. They get the same pests and diseases, which build up in the soil.
seasoned: Avoid planting cantaloupe where any cucurbit grew in the last few years, including cucumber, watermelon, squash, and pumpkin. They share cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it carries, the mildews, and especially the soilborne Fusarium wilt and debris- and seed-borne gummy stem blight and Alternaria, which build up in the soil and on residue.

beginner: Try not to grow cantaloupe or its relatives (cucumbers, melons, squash) in the same spot more than once every 3 years, and wait longer if you have had wilt or leaf disease. Moving them around the garden helps avoid a buildup of soil and debris diseases. Note that this does not stop bacterial wilt, which comes from beetles, not the soil. Clean up old vines at the end of the season too.
seasoned: Rotate cantaloupe and its cucurbit relatives on at least a 3 year cycle, and stretch it where Fusarium wilt or gummy stem blight are established, since the muskmelon wilt fungus persists in soil for years and the foliar diseases carry over on debris and seed. A long rotation is an important cultural defense, though it does not touch bacterial wilt, which arrives on beetles rather than from the soil. Clear and remove spent vines at season's end rather than tilling them in, which removes overwintering disease sites.

beginner: Give cantaloupe about 1 to 2 inches of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day, since the plant roots deep and the fruit is mostly water.
seasoned: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches of water per week, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. Cantaloupe is deep-rooted and the fruit is largely water, so steady moisture through vining and fruit sizing is essential, but the plant also wants a dry finish to sweeten.

beginner: About 1 to 2 inches of water a week is a good target, more while the plant is flowering and the melons are growing.
seasoned: Around 1 to 2 inches per week is the working range (Iowa State suggests 1 to 2 inches every 7 to 10 days in dry weather), leaning higher during flowering and fruit sizing and through hot, dry spells. Even, deep watering builds full, well-shaped melons; let the plant swing dry and you get poor set, small fruit, and misshapen melons.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, using a soaker hose or watering wand at the base, which helps prevent leaf disease. As the melons get close to ripe, ease off the water. That last step is what makes cantaloupe sweet, since too much water near harvest waters down the flavor and can crack the fruit.
seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves invite the mildews, gummy stem blight, and Alternaria that cantaloupe is prone to. It wants full sun, warm soil, and a long warm season of roughly 75 to 90 days, and it does not begin in earnest until the ground is reliably warm, so most gardeners either wait for warm soil to direct sow or set out transplants started about three weeks ahead. The single most important thing to learn is the harvest call: cantaloupe is picked once per fruit, at full slip, when the stem separates cleanly from the melon under light thumb pressure, backed up by coarse raised netting, a background skin that turns from green to tan under the net, and a sweet musky aroma at the stem end. Picked at full slip it is at peak sweetness; picked early it will soften and grow aromatic but never actually sweeten, since the sugar is set on the vine. The crop's defining trouble is disease: cantaloupe is one of the most bacterial-wilt-susceptible cucurbits, far more than watermelon, so keeping cucumber beetles off young plants is the whole game, and it is also prey to Fusarium wilt, gummy stem blight, Alternaria, and the powdery and downy mildews. Give it heat, room to sprawl, bees for pollination, even water through sizing and a dry finish to sweeten, and cool-summer northern and foggy-coastal gardeners should lean on early varieties, transplants, and black plastic mulch.

Read full slip alongside the other signs, which come on together in the last few days: the netting stands up coarse and corky over the whole fruit; the background skin between the netting turns from green to tan, buff, or yellow; a sweet, musky aroma rises at the blossom and stem end; and the tendril nearest the fruit dries and browns. Harvest at full slip for peak sweetness, since cantaloupe does not gain sugar after picking, though it will soften and grow more fragrant on the counter. Because a full-slip melon over-ripens on the vine within a day or two, check ripening melons daily as slip approaches; if you want to hold or ship a melon, pick a hair early at half slip, when the stem is just starting to separate. Lift the melon free with a light thumb push at the stem, or cut it leaving a short stub, then refrigerate promptly since it does not store long.
